title: Mentha
wiki_lead:
Mentha, also known as mint (from Greek μίνθα míntha, Linear B mi-ta), is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae. It is estimated that 18 to 24 species exist, but the exact distinction between species is unclear. Hybridization occurs naturally where some species' ranges overlap. Many hybrids and cultivars are known.
The genus has a subcosmopolitan distribution, growing best in wet environments and moist soils.
wiki_excerpt:
Mentha, also known as mint (from Greek μίνθα míntha, Linear B mi-ta), is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae. It is estimated that 18 to 24 species exist, but the exact distinction between species is unclear. Hybridization occurs naturally where some species' ranges overlap. Many hybrids and cultivars are known.
The genus has a subcosmopolitan distribution, growing best in wet environments and moist soils.


Description

Mints are aromatic, almost exclusively perennial herbs. They have wide-spreading underground and overground stolons and erect, square, branched stems. Mints will grow 10–120 cm (4–47 in) tall and can spread over an indeterminate area. Due to their tendency to spread unchecked, some mints are considered invasive.
The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs, from oblong to lanceolate, often downy, and with a serrated margin. Leaf colours range from dark green and gray-green to purple, blue, and sometimes pale yellow.
The flowers are produced in long bracts from leaf axils. They are white to purple and produced in false whorls called verticillasters. The corolla is two-lipped with four subequal lobes, the upper lobe usually the largest. The fruit is a nutlet, containing one to four seeds.


Taxonomy
Mentha is a member of the tribe Mentheae in the subfamily Nepetoideae. The tribe contains about 65 genera, and relationships within it remain obscure. Authors have disagreed on the circumscription of Mentha. For example, M. cervina has been placed in Pulegium and Preslia, and M. cunninghamii has been placed in Micromeria. In 2004, a molecular phylogenetic study indicated that both M. cervina and M. cunninghamii should be included in Mentha. However, M. cunninghamii was excluded in a 2007 treatment of the genus.
More than 3,000 names have been published in the genus Mentha, at ranks from species to forms, the majority of which are regarded as synonyms or illegitimate names. The taxonomy of the genus is made difficult because many species hybridize readily, or are themselves derived from possibly ancient hybridization events. Seeds from hybrids give rise to variable offspring, which may spread through vegetative propagation. The variability has led to what has been described as "paroxysms of species and subspecific taxa"; for example, one taxonomist published 434 new mint taxa for central Europe alone between 1911 and 1916. Recent sources recognize between 18 and 24 species.

grok_lead: Mentha is a genus of approximately 25 species of aromatic, perennial herbaceous plants in the family Lamiaceae, native to the temperate regions of Europe, Asia, and Africa. These plants are characterized by square stems, opposite or whorled leaves with serrated margins, and small tubular to bell-shaped flowers typically arranged in dense clusters or verticillasters. They reproduce both vegetatively through spreading underground rhizomes or runners and by seed, often forming extensive colonies in moist, sunny habitats such as stream banks and wetlands. The genus is notable for its high degree of hybridization, resulting in numerous natural and cultivated hybrids, with estimates of up to 42 species, 15 hybrids, and many subspecies or varieties recognized in taxonomy. It is classified into five sections: Audibertia, Eriodontes, Mentha, Preslia, and Pulegium. Mentha species produce essential oils rich in monoterpenes such as menthol, carvone, and pulegone, secreted by glandular trichomes on leaves and stems, which impart their characteristic fragrances and flavors. Widely distributed and naturalized globally, including in North America, Australia, and other regions, Mentha plants originated in the Mediterranean basin and thrive in diverse environments from sea level to montane areas. Economically significant, they are cultivated on large scales in countries like the United States, India, and China for essential oil production used in food flavoring (e.g., teas, confectionery), pharmaceuticals (e.g., for gastrointestinal disorders and analgesics), cosmetics, and as natural preservatives due to their antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. Prominent species include Mentha spicata (spearmint), Mentha aquatica (water mint), Mentha canadensis (American wild mint), and the sterile hybrid Mentha Ã piperita (peppermint), which dominates commercial production.
